pos: adj. & v. (spoiled, rotten, morally depraved; rendering Hebrew shachath, Greek phtheirō)
etymology: From Latin corruptus, from com and rumpere, to break to pieces. Corruption in Scripture is not damage from outside but decay working from within.
biblical_def: Corrupt in Scripture names decay working from the inside out, and it is applied first to the race and then to everything the race handles. Before the flood the verdict is total: “God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth” (Gen 6:12) — corrupt in condition and corrupting in action, the two inseparable. The psalmist gives the same diagnosis without a flood to prove it: “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good” (Psa 14:1), which Paul quotes in Romans 3 as the settled state of man apart from grace. Paul names the mechanism in the individual: the old man “is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts” (Eph 4:22) — the desires themselves are the agents of the rot, and they lie about it while they work. And our Lord extends the principle to possessions: treasure laid up on earth is where “moth and rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:19). Everything under the fall is decaying, including the things men store up against decay.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines corrupt as changed from a sound to a putrid state; spoiled; tainted; vitiated in mind; and depraved, wicked, or bribed.
webster_full: CORRUPT, a. Changed from a sound to a putrid or putrescent state; spoiled; tainted; vitiated; unsound.
2. Changed from a state of uprightness, correctness, truth, etc. to a bad state; vitiated; depraved; debased; perverted.
3. Not genuine; infected with errors or mistakes.
CORRUPT, v.t. To change from a sound to a putrid or putrescent state.
2. To vitiate or deprave; to destroy integrity.
scriptures: Gen 6:12
And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.
Psa 14:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
Eph 4:22
That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;
Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
corruption_summary: Sin has been redefined as damage sustained rather than corruption possessed, so that man is treated as fundamentally sound and externally injured — which is precisely what Genesis 6 and Psalm 14 deny.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant modern account of human wrongdoing is environmental: people are essentially good and are harmed, deprived, or conditioned into bad behaviour, so the remedy is better circumstances. Scripture's word is corrupt, and it locates the trouble in the nature rather than the surroundings. All flesh had corrupted his way; there is none that doeth good; the old man is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts. Total depravity does not mean every man is as bad as he could be — it means no part of him is undamaged, including the will that would have to choose the remedy.

The pastoral difference is enormous. On the environmental account, a man needs improvement, and the church becomes a programme. On the biblical account, a man needs a new nature, and the church preaches a new birth. Ephesians 4 does not tell the Christian to renovate the old man but to put him off and put on the new man, created in righteousness and true holiness. And Matthew 6 removes the last hiding place: even the treasure a man corrupts himself to accumulate is quietly rotting in the box.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath (H7843), to corrupt, mar, destroy; Greek phtheirō (G5351), to spoil or ruin, and aphanizō (G853), to make disappear — decay working from within.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to spoil, ruin, corrupt; used twice in Gen 6:12 of both the state and the act.
Greek phtheirō (G5351) — to corrupt, defile, destroy; the old man corrupt according to deceitful lusts (Eph 4:22).
Greek aphanizō (G853) — to cause to vanish, consume; the moth and rust that corrupt earthly treasure (Mat 6:19).
usage: “All flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth” — the condition and the conduct together.
“They are corrupt… there is none that doeth good” — Paul's proof text for universal depravity.
“Where moth and rust doth corrupt” — the hedge against decay is itself decaying.

pos: adj. (perished, missing, ruined; rendering Hebrew abad, Greek apollumi)
etymology: Past participle of lose, Saxon losian. In Scripture lost is not a description of confusion but of ruin — and it is the word Christ chose for His own mission statement.
biblical_def: Lost is the word our Lord used to summarise why He came: “For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luk 19:10) — spoken over Zacchaeus's dinner table, to a man the crowd had already written off. It is not a gentle word. The same root is translated perish, and Paul uses it of those under judgment: “if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost” (2Co 4:3). But the same word carries the tenderest scene in the Gospels, the shepherd home with the sheep on his shoulders: “Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost” (Luk 15:6). And behind both stands the promise God made through Ezekiel when the shepherds of Israel had failed: “I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick” (Eze 34:16). The lost do not find themselves. They are sought, and by a Shepherd who counts, goes out, and comes home rejoicing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lost as parted with, no longer possessed, missing, ruined or destroyed, and in a moral sense wasted or forfeited.
webster_full: LOST, pp. Mislaid or left in a place unknown or forgotten; that cannot be found.
2. Ruined; destroyed; wasted or squandered.
3. Forfeited; as a lost estate.
4. Not perceptible to the senses; no longer visible.
5. Bewildered; perplexed; as, a man is lost in his own reasoning.
scriptures: For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
Luk 15:6
And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.
But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost:

I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment.
corruption_summary: “Lost” has been softened into a synonym for searching or spiritually curious, which removes the danger the word was chosen to convey and turns the Shepherd's errand into an escort service.
corruption_paragraphs: In common religious speech a lost person is one still on a journey, exploring, not yet arrived — language that flatters everyone and warns no one. The Greek is apollumi, the same verb translated perish in John 3:16, and it means ruin, not itinerancy. A lost sheep in Palestine did not wander philosophically; it died of exposure or was eaten. Preaching that will not say the word plainly cannot preach the rescue plainly either, because a man who does not know he is perishing sees no reason to be carried home.

Ezekiel 34 fixes the responsibility before Luke 15 shows the joy. God's indictment there is against shepherds who fed themselves and did not seek the lost, and His answer is to come and do it Himself. That is the standard for every under-shepherd: not merely tending the ninety and nine who are pleasant to tend, but going out after the one. And the mark that a church has understood the word is the sound Luke describes — friends and neighbours called together, and rejoicing that seems disproportionate to everyone who has forgotten what lost meant.
roots_summary: Hebrew abad (H6), to perish, be lost, destroyed; Greek apollumi (G622), to destroy fully or to perish — the same verb rendered perish in John 3:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew abad (H6) — to perish, wander away, be lost; “I will seek that which was lost” (Eze 34:16).
Greek apollumi (G622) — to destroy, lose utterly, perish; the lost sheep (Luk 15:6) and the lost of 2Co 4:3.
The participle in Luk 19:10 is neuter — that which was lost — taking in the whole ruined estate of man, not a category of people.
usage: “To seek and to save that which was lost” — the Lord's own summary of His errand.
“I have found my sheep which was lost” — the sheep is carried, not led.
“It is hid to them that are lost” — the word's hard edge, kept.

pos: adj. (deprived of courage, appalled; rendering Hebrew chathath)
etymology: From the old French, to deprive of might or courage. In Scripture it is the specific fear God most often forbids by name, and He forbids it with a reason attached.
biblical_def: Dismayed is fear that has taken the strength out of a man, and it is the word God most often couples with His prohibition of fear. To Israel in exile: “Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness” (Isa 41:10) — four promises attached to two commands, because God never tells a man not to be dismayed without telling him why. To Joshua at the Jordan: “Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Jos 1:9). To a young prophet facing a hostile nation: “be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them” (Jer 1:17) — a solemn warning that fear of men invites the very humiliation it dreads. And the negative example: when Goliath spoke, “Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid” (1Sa 17:11). An army with a covenant, undone by a voice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dismay as to deprive of that strength or firmness of mind which constitutes courage; to discourage; to dishearten; to affright.
webster_full: DISMAY, v.t. To deprive of that strength or firmness of mind which constitutes courage; to discourage; to dishearten; to sink or depress the spirits.
DISMAY, n. Loss of courage; depression of spirits; consternation.
DISMAYED, pp. Deprived of courage; disheartened; affrighted.
DISMAYEDNESS, n. A state of being dismayed; dejection of courage.
scriptures: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Jer 1:17
Thou therefore gird up thy loins, and arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them.
When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid.
corruption_summary: The command not to be dismayed is heard as a demand to feel differently, which is impossible; Scripture attaches a reason to every such command, and the reason is the cure.
corruption_paragraphs: Told simply to stop being afraid, a frightened man either pretends or despairs. Scripture never issues the command bare. Be not dismayed, for I am thy God. Be not dismayed, for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest. The imperative rests on an indicative, and the work of faith is not to manufacture a feeling but to believe the clause after the comma. This is why bare exhortation fails in the pulpit and in the home: courage is a by-product of a known promise, not a virtue summoned by effort.

Jeremiah 1:17 adds the warning that keeps this from being merely comforting. Be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them — the fear of man is not a harmless weakness but an invitation to the very confusion the fearful man is trying to avoid. And 1 Samuel 17 shows the corporate version: an entire covenant nation dismayed by one loud Philistine, until a shepherd boy arrived who had done his arithmetic differently. Nothing had changed about Goliath. Something was different about who David was counting on.
roots_summary: Hebrew chathath (H2865), to be shattered, dismayed, broken down with fear — the collapse of courage, and the fear God most often forbids by name.
roots_lines: Hebrew chathath (H2865) — to be broken, shattered, dismayed; “be not dismayed” (Isa 41:10; Jos 1:9; Jer 1:17).
The same root describes bows broken (1Sa 2:4) — dismay is a man's courage snapped like a weapon.
Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear; regularly paired with chathath in the double command fear not, neither be dismayed.
usage: “Be not dismayed; for I am thy God” — the command with its reason attached.
“Be not dismayed at their faces” — fear of man invites the confusion it dreads.
“They were dismayed, and greatly afraid” — a covenant army undone by a voice.

pos: adj. (struck with amazement or awe; rendering Hebrew shamem, Greek ekplēssō)
etymology: From Latin attonare, to thunder-strike. The old sense is stronger than modern surprise — to be struck as by a thunderclap.
biblical_def: To be astonished in the Authorized Version is to be thunderstruck, and the Gospels use it chiefly of what happened to people when Christ opened His mouth. After the Sermon on the Mount: “when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine” (Mat 7:28) — and the next verse gives the reason, for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. At twelve years old in the temple the effect was already present: “all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers” (Luk 2:47). Sometimes the astonishment is dismay at a doctrine too hard: when Christ said it was easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom, “they were astonished out of measure, saying among themselves, Who then can be saved?” (Mar 10:26) — and His answer, that with God all things are possible, is the doctrine of grace given to men who had just discovered they could not save themselves. Astonishment is the honest reaction of a creature to a word from outside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines astonish as to stun, to strike dumb with sudden fear, terror, surprise or wonder — the mind being for a moment overpowered.
webster_full: ASTONISH, v.t. To stun or strike dumb with sudden fear, terror, surprise or wonder; to amaze; to confound with some sudden passion.
ASTONISHED, pp. Amazed; confounded with fear, surprise, or admiration.
ASTONISHMENT, n. Amazement; confusion of mind from fear, surprise or admiration, at an extraordinary or unexpected event.
scriptures: Mat 7:28
And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine:
Luk 2:47
And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers.
And they were astonished out of measure, saying among themselves, Who then can be saved?
Isa 53:1
Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the LORD revealed?
corruption_summary: Astonishment has been demoted to entertainment — a reaction the pulpit tries to produce by novelty — where the Gospels report it as the effect of plain authority in the teaching of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew is careful to say what the people were astonished at: his doctrine. Not staging, not delivery, not an unexpected illustration. The wonder came from the content and from the fact that He spoke as one having authority, unlike the scribes who could only cite other men. Preaching that seeks astonishment by other means — production, spectacle, cleverness — may get a reaction, but not this one. The reaction Matthew names is available only to preaching that says what God has said and does not hedge it.

Mark 10 shows the other half. Real astonishment is often unpleasant, because it comes from hearing a demand that flattens one's assumptions. The disciples were astonished out of measure and asked who then can be saved — a question that only occurs to someone whose confidence has just failed. A ministry that never leaves anyone asking that question has probably never astonished anyone in the biblical sense, however impressive its effects.
roots_summary: Hebrew shamem (H8074), to be desolate or appalled; Greek ekplēssō (G1605), to strike out of one's senses — the effect of authority in speech.
roots_lines: Greek ekplēssō (G1605) — to strike with astonishment, drive out of one's wits; the crowds at the Sermon (Mat 7:28) and in the temple (Luk 2:47).
Greek ekplessomai in Mar 10:26 is intensified — astonished out of measure — at the impossibility of self-salvation.
Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, stunned, appalled; the prophets' word for men struck silent before God's doing.
usage: “The people were astonished at his doctrine” — at the doctrine, and at the authority.
“Astonished at his understanding and answers” — at twelve years old.
“Astonished out of measure, saying… Who then can be saved?” — the useful kind of astonishment.

etymology: From Latin refusare, to pour back, decline. Scripture uses the word for the noblest refusal in Hebrews 11 and for the most fatal refusal in Proverbs 1.
biblical_def: Refusal in Scripture cuts in both directions, and everything depends on what is refused. There is a refusal that is faith's finest act: “By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter” (Heb 11:24) — a man declining a throne because he had seen something better. There is the refusal that condemned the builders and became the cornerstone of the gospel: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psa 118:22), quoted by Christ against the chief priests and by Peter before the Sanhedrin. There is the refusal wisdom warns of: “Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” (Pro 1:24) — and the chapter goes on to a silence that answers in kind. And Hebrews presses the point to its sharpest edge: “See that ye refuse not him that speaketh. For if they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape, if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven” (Heb 12:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refuse as to deny a request, demand or invitation; to decline to accept an offer; and to reject, to decline to do or grant.
webster_full: REFUSE, v.t. To deny a request, demand, invitation or command; to decline to do or grant.
2. To decline to accept what is offered; as, to refuse an office.
3. To reject; to dismiss.
REFUSE, v.i. To decline to accept; not to comply.
REFUSED, pp. Denied; rejected; not accepted.
scriptures: By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter;
The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
Pro 1:24
Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded;
See that ye refuse not him that speaketh. For if they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape, if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven:
corruption_summary: Refusal is treated as inherently negative — closed-mindedness, exclusion — where Scripture makes the direction of the refusal the whole question, and honours Moses for the greatest No in the Old Testament.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture whose highest virtue is openness has trouble with a Bible that praises a man for saying no. Hebrews 11 lists Moses' refusal among the great acts of faith: he declined the standing, wealth, and identity that Egypt held out, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. That is not narrowness; it is arithmetic, and Hebrews shows his working — he had respect unto the recompence of the reward. Every faithful refusal in Scripture is made by someone who has priced both options.

Proverbs 1 and Hebrews 12 supply the terrible symmetry. The man who refuses wisdom's call will one day call and not be answered; the man who refuses Him that speaketh from heaven has no second court of appeal. And Psalm 118 shows what happens to the thing men refuse: the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner. Refusal does not dispose of Christ. It only determines whether a man meets Him as foundation or as the stone that falls.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'en (H3985), to refuse, and ma'as (H3988), to reject or despise; Greek arneomai (G720), to deny, and paraiteomai (G3868), to decline or beg off.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'as (H3988) — to refuse, reject, despise; “the stone which the builders refused” (Psa 118:22).
Hebrew ma'en (H3985) — to refuse, be unwilling; “I have called, and ye refused” (Pro 1:24).
Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, disown, refuse; Moses refusing the name of Pharaoh's daughter (Heb 11:24).
usage: “Refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter” — faith declining a throne.
“The stone which the builders refused” — refusal did not dispose of Him.
“See that ye refuse not him that speaketh” — and there is no higher court.

pos: adj. (disposed, ready of mind, consenting; rendering Hebrew nedabah, Greek prothumos, boulomai)
etymology: From will, Saxon willan. Willingness in Scripture is a disposition God creates in His people, not a resource they contribute.
biblical_def: Willing describes a ready disposition, and Scripture is careful about where it comes from. Of God's patience: “The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2Pe 3:9). Of God's people, and note the passive construction: “Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning” (Psa 110:3) — the willingness arrives with the power, and the psalm is about the King's conquest, not the subject's initiative. Of Christian giving, where willingness rather than amount is the measure: “if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not” (2Co 8:12). And of the honest limits of a willing man: “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mat 26:41) — said not as an excuse for the sleeping disciples but as the reason they were commanded to watch and pray.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines willing as free to do or grant, disposed, not averse, ready, and consenting — done or offered of choice or without reluctance.
webster_full: WILLING, a. Free to do or grant; having the mind inclined; disposed; not averse.
2. Ready; prompt.
3. Chosen; received of choice or without reluctance.
4. Spontaneous.
WILLINGLY, adv. With free will; without reluctance; cheerfully.
scriptures: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: thou hast the dew of thy youth.
For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
corruption_summary: 2 Peter 3:9 is routinely read as a statement about God's frustrated desire for every individual, detaching it from the us-ward Peter actually wrote and turning divine patience into divine inability.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is quoted as though it read not willing that any of mankind should perish, and made to prove that God's saving will is universal and regularly defeated. Peter's own words limit the scope: he is longsuffering to us-ward, writing to them that have obtained like precious faith, explaining why the promised coming has not yet arrived — because the elect are not all gathered in. The verse is about the timing of the second advent, and its comfort is that no one for whom Christ died will be missed because the Lord came early. Definite atonement and this verse are not in conflict; the verse is one of its supports.

Psalm 110 then settles the question of where human willingness originates. Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power — not if they are willing He will exert power, but the willingness is the visible effect of the power. This is effectual calling stated in five words, and it is why 2 Corinthians 8 can make a willing mind the measure of acceptable giving without turning it into a work. The willingness God accepts is the willingness God gave.
roots_summary: Hebrew nedabah (H5071), a freewill offering or voluntariness; Greek prothumos (G4289), ready of mind, and boulomai (G1014), to will or purpose.
roots_lines: Hebrew nedabah (H5071) — voluntariness, freewill offering; behind “thy people shall be willing” (Psa 110:3).
Greek prothumos (G4289) — ready, eager, willing; “the spirit indeed is willing” (Mat 26:41).
Greek boulomai (G1014) — to will, purpose, be minded; “not willing that any should perish” (2Pe 3:9).
usage: “Not willing that any should perish” — read with Peter's own us-ward.
“Thy people shall be willing in the day of thy power” — the willingness follows the power.
“If there be first a willing mind, it is accepted” — measured by readiness, not by amount.

pos: v.i. (to remain, persist, abide; rendering Greek menō, epimenō, proskartereō)
etymology: From Latin continuare, to join without break. In the New Testament continuance is the ordinary test of reality — not how a profession began, but whether it lasted.
biblical_def: To continue is to remain in a thing without break, and the New Testament makes it the standing evidence of genuine faith. Our Lord said it to men who had just believed on Him: “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31) — discipleship proved by remaining, not by the initial response. Paul says the same of the whole gospel hope: reconciliation is presented to God “if ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel” (Col 1:23). The Jerusalem church shows what continuance looks like in practice, and it is unspectacular: “they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — four things, done again and again. And Paul forecloses the abuse of the doctrine of grace with the same verb: “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” (Rom 6:1). One kind of continuing proves life; the other proves its absence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines continue as to remain in a state or place, to last, to persevere, to be steadfast or constant in any course.
webster_full: CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely.
2. To last; to be durable; to endure; to be permanent.
3. To persevere; to be steadfast or constant in any course.
CONTINUE, v.t. To protract; not to cease from or to terminate.
2. To extend from one thing to another; to produce or draw out in length.
scriptures: Joh 8:31
Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;
Col 1:23

If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, and which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister;
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Rom 6:1
What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
corruption_summary: Continuance has been made optional by a doctrine of bare decisionism, in which a past profession settles the matter and perseverance is treated as an extra for the keen.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary holds the perseverance of the saints, and precisely for that reason it will not accept the counterfeit that goes by the same territory. Bare once saved always saved treats a recorded decision as the whole of the question and makes continuing irrelevant; the Confession, with Scripture, teaches that those whom God has accepted in the Beloved can neither totally nor finally fall away, and that this shows itself in their continuing. John 8:31 and Colossians 1:23 are not threats to assurance but its instruments: the man who continues has the evidence in hand.

Acts 2:42 keeps the doctrine from becoming abstract, and the list is deliberately ordinary — doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayers. Perseverance is not a heroic posture maintained under floodlights; it is showing up, hearing the Word, taking the Supper, and praying, for decades. Romans 6:1 then closes the other door. The grace that guarantees continuance in Christ is the same grace that makes continuance in sin unthinkable, and Paul's answer to the question is God forbid.
roots_summary: Greek menō (G3306), to abide or remain, epimenō (G1961), to continue in, and proskartereō (G4342), to persist steadfastly — the evidence of a real work.
roots_lines: Greek menō (G3306) — to abide, remain, continue; “if ye continue in my word” (Joh 8:31), and the abiding of Joh 15.
Greek epimenō (G1961) — to remain in, persist; “if ye continue in the faith” (Col 1:23), and “shall we continue in sin” (Rom 6:1).
Greek proskartereō (G4342) — to attend constantly, persevere; the fourfold continuance of Act 2:42.
usage: “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” — the test is remaining.
“They continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” — four ordinary things, repeated.
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” — the other continuance, forbidden.

pos: v. & n. (to rest upon, to support, to remain; rendering Hebrew samak, sha'an)
etymology: From the old French, to prop or support. The Authorized Version's stay is usually not remain but lean — the weight of a thing resting on a support.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version to stay most often means to lean or rest one's weight upon something, and Isaiah builds a doctrine on it. Of the settled mind: “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee” (Isa 26:3) — peace is not a temperament but the result of where the mind has put its weight. Of the remnant that learned the lesson: they “shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth” (Isa 10:20), Judah having leaned on Assyria and been struck by the very prop it chose. And of brothers holding up a man who cannot hold himself up: on the hill above the battle, “Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun” (Exo 17:12). A man may stay on God and still need two men to stay up his arms. Scripture sees no contradiction there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stay as to prop, to hold up, to support; and as that which supports or upholds, a prop or buttress — as well as to remain or continue.
webster_full: STAY, v.t. To stop; to hold from proceeding; to withhold; to restrain.
2. To delay; to obstruct; to hinder from proceeding.
3. To prop; to hold up; to support.
STAY, n. That which supports or holds up; a prop; a buttress.
2. Continuance in a place; abode for a time indefinite.
scriptures: Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the remnant of Israel, and such as are escaped of the house of Jacob, shall no more again stay upon him that smote them; but shall stay upon the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.

But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:
corruption_summary: Peace is pursued as an inner technique of calming the mind, where Isaiah makes it the by-product of the mind's object — kept in perfect peace because it is stayed on Someone.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern search for peace is largely a search for a method: quieting, breathing, emptying, managing the racing thought. Isaiah 26:3 offers no method at all, and its grammar is worth attending to — Thou wilt keep him. The keeping is God's act; the man's part is where he leans. A mind stayed on God is not a mind that has learned to stop thinking but one that has settled its weight on a Person, and the peace follows as a consequence rather than as an achievement. Techniques that leave the object of trust unchanged can quiet a mind for an hour; they cannot keep it.

Isaiah 10:20 supplies the warning, and it is a political one as much as a personal one. Judah leaned on Assyria for protection and was smitten by Assyria, and the remnant's recovery is described as no longer staying on him that smote them. Every generation has its Assyria — an alliance, an institution, a strong man — and the pattern holds: what a people leans on instead of God eventually strikes them. Exodus 17 then keeps the doctrine warm. Moses stayed on God and still needed Aaron and Hur under each arm, which is exactly what the local church is for.
roots_summary: Hebrew samak (H5564), to lean, lay, uphold, and sha'an (H8172), to lean or rest upon — the weight of a life placed on a support.
roots_lines: Hebrew samak (H5564) — to lean, lay (a hand), sustain; “whose mind is stayed on thee” (Isa 26:3), and the hand laid on the sacrifice.
Hebrew sha'an (H8172) — to lean, rely; “shall stay upon the LORD” (Isa 10:20), and “lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5).
Hebrew tamak (H8551) — to grasp, hold up, sustain; behind Aaron and Hur staying up Moses' hands (Exo 17:12).
usage: “Whose mind is stayed on thee” — peace named as a consequence of leaning.
“Shall no more again stay upon him that smote them” — the alliance that struck them.
“Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands” — a man leaning on God and on two brothers.

pos: v.t. (to look upon, to esteem, to have respect unto; rendering Hebrew ra'ah, shur, Greek epiblepō, ameleō)
etymology: From the French regarder, to look at. In Scripture regarding is never neutral looking; it is looking with esteem, and God's regard falls where men do not expect it.
biblical_def: To regard is to look upon a thing with esteem, and Scripture uses it to describe where God's eye rests and what a man's eye is fixed on. Mary's song reports God's direction of gaze: “he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luk 1:48) — He looked at the least likely house in Israel. The psalmist reports the fatal direction of a man's own gaze: “If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Psa 66:18) — not the presence of sin, which is in every heart, but sin regarded, cherished, held on to and looked at with favour. Wisdom records being ignored: “I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” (Pro 1:24). And Hebrews quotes God's reciprocal withdrawal from a covenant-breaking generation: “because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord” (Heb 8:9). Whom God regards and what a man regards are the two questions the word puts, and the second decides whether prayer is heard.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines regard as to look towards, to observe, to esteem, to have respect to, and to pay attention to as a matter of importance.
webster_full: REGARD, v.t. To look towards; to point or be directed.
2. To observe; to notice with some particularity.
3. To attend to with respect and estimation; to value.
4. To attend to as a thing that affects our interest.
5. To keep; to observe with religious or solemn attention.
scriptures: Luk 1:48
For he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden: for, behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.
If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:
Pro 1:24
Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded;
Heb 8:9

Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they continued not in my covenant, and I regarded them not, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Psalm 66:18 is heard as a threat that any remaining sin blocks prayer, which drives sincere believers to despair; the verse is about sin regarded — cherished and looked at with favour — not sin present and fought.
corruption_paragraphs: The misreading is common and it wounds tender consciences. If the verse meant that a man with any sin in his heart cannot be heard, no prayer would ever ascend, since indwelling sin remains in the holiest believer until glory. The Hebrew is about looking at iniquity with approval — keeping it in view, guarding it, refusing to part with it. A Christian who hates his sin, confesses it, and fights it is not the man described; the man described is the one who has made peace with a sin and prays anyway. The difference is the whole difference between David in Psalm 51 and Saul at Endor.

Luke 1:48 supplies the encouraging half of the doctrine. God regards the low estate — the unimportant house, the unnoticed servant, the congregation nobody writes about. This is a settled pattern rather than an exception: He resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble, and He chose the weak things of the world to confound the mighty. Where a man's eye rests determines whether he is heard; where God's eye rests is settled by grace, and it has never yet rested where the world expected.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, look upon, regard; Greek epiblepō (G1914), to look upon with favour, and ameleō (G272), to be careless of — the direction of the eye, divine and human.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, look at, regard; “if I regard iniquity in my heart” (Psa 66:18).
Greek epiblepō (G1914) — to look upon, regard with favour; “he hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden” (Luk 1:48).
Greek ameleō (G272) — to neglect, be unconcerned; “I regarded them not” (Heb 8:9).
usage: “He hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden” — where God's eye rests.
“If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” — sin cherished, not sin present.
“I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded” — wisdom ignored.

pos: adj. (pierced, hurt, injured; rendering Hebrew chalal, nakah, Greek traumatizō)
etymology: From Saxon wund, a hurt. Isaiah 53 makes the word the hinge of substitution: He wounded, and by His stripes we healed.
biblical_def: Wounded in Scripture is the language of substitution and of the soul's deepest injury. Isaiah states the exchange in one verse: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5) — four clauses, and in each the wound is His and the benefit is ours. Zechariah adds a strange and haunting detail of the smitten Shepherd: “What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends” (Zec 13:6). Proverbs then names the injury no medicine reaches: “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?” (Pro 18:14) — a man's inner strength carries his bodily weakness, but when the inner man himself is wounded there is nothing left underneath to do the carrying. The answer to that question is the first verse: the only cure for a wounded spirit is a wounded Saviour, and the stripes that heal are His.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wound as a breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark of a plant, caused by violence; and figuratively an injury to reputation or to the feelings.
webster_full: WOUND, n. A breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark and wood of a tree, or of the bark and substance of other plants, caused by violence or external force.
2. Injury; hurt; as a wound given to credit or reputation.
WOUND, v.t. To hurt by violence; as, to wound the head or the arm.
2. To hurt the feelings; to pain.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Zec 13:6
And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.
The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear?
He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
corruption_summary: The wounded spirit has been transferred wholesale to the clinic, and the church has largely accepted the transfer — ceding a category Scripture treats as spiritual and answers with a wounded Christ. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic frame to reject it -->
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 18:14 asks a question the modern age answers almost entirely in one register: a wounded spirit is a condition to be assessed, named, and managed, and the pastor's role shrinks to referral. Some of that referral is right — bodies affect souls, and Scripture never despises ordinary means or the physician. But a church that has no category of its own for a wounded spirit has surrendered the very thing it exists to address, and it will have nothing to say when the assessment is complete and the man is still in the dark. <!-- voice-lock-ok: therapy: rebuttal context -->

Scripture's answer is not a technique but a Person with wounds. Isaiah 53 does not merely sympathise with the injured; it says the injury was transferred — wounded for our transgressions, and with his stripes we are healed. Zechariah's detail is that the wounds were received in the house of His friends, which means He is not a stranger to being hurt by those closest to Him. The psalmist puts it plainly: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds. Binding up is slow, deliberate work, and He is described as doing it Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalal (H2490), to pierce or wound fatally, and nakah (H5221), to smite; Greek traumatizō (G5135), to wound — the pierced Servant and the pierced spirit.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to pierce, wound, profane; “he was wounded for our transgressions” (Isa 53:5).
Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to strike, smite, wound; the smitten Shepherd of Zec 13:7.
Hebrew nakeh (H5218) with ruach — a stricken or wounded spirit (Pro 18:14), the injury that leaves nothing underneath to carry the man.
usage: “He was wounded for our transgressions” — the wound His, the healing ours.
“Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends” — hurt by the nearest.
“A wounded spirit who can bear?” — the question only a wounded Saviour answers.
